description: Width tiers for Design and Technologies Years 1-2 (ACARA v9). One entry per descriptor.
subject: Design and Technologies

generation_rules.notes: K-strand descriptors (K01–K04) use phenomena_contexts. P-strand descriptors (P01–P04) use task_contexts. First Nations elaborations present in K01, K02, K03, K04. AC9TDE2P02 has some thin width at node level for safe tool use — consolidation is the primary response there.

width_notes.minimum: The narrowest context or task that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. Every student in the class meets this floor before the class moves on.
width_notes.typical: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice for the band.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena or task contexts, not difficulty. Each item is a concrete direction for advancing students. First Nations elaborations included as default wider directions where ACARA provides them.

AC9TDE2K01.minimum_width: Identify one community need and explain how a product, service or environment is designed to meet it; identify one sustainability consideration in a design context.
AC9TDE2K01.typical_width: Identify community needs across health, shelter, food, communication and community access contexts; explain design and production decisions that address each need; identify sustainability considerations including waste minimisation and care for living systems.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians have long understood their dependence on living systems — for example how the Ngarrindjeri Peoples sustainably make woven items from a grass-like sedge; identify the community need and how the design reflects sustainability
Ask questions about the design of shelters in public spaces (school, sportsground) — identify the community need and how design decisions address it including accessibility considerations
Explore how people modify existing designs to prevent water wastage — identify the sustainability problem, the design response and how it minimises environmental impact
elaborations: exploring how First Nations Australians have long understood their dependence on living systems to meet their local and community needs, for example exploring the material culture of the Ngarrindjeri Peoples who sustainably make woven items from a grass-like sedge

exploring how particular services meet different needs of people in the community, for example describing why doctors provide medical care to people in many ways including by phone, video conference, plane, car or outdoor clinic

asking questions about the design of a range of shelters provided for the public and how they meet the needs of people in the community, for example the structures of a school or local sportsground or how to improve accessibility

exploring how local products are designed, for example brainstorming the materials and processes needed to create a costume for a school or community event including using recycled clothing or components to minimise waste
exploring how people come up with new ideas or modify existing designs, for example preventing water wastage when caring for plants

AC9TDE2K02.minimum_width: Identify at least one material property and explain how it affects movement in a product; identify one force and explain how it combines with a material to create movement.
AC9TDE2K02.typical_width: Explore multiple material properties and explain how each affects movement; select materials deliberately for movement outcomes (sliding, floating, flying); explain how combining materials with forces creates movement across multiple products.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' instructive toys — for example propeller toys made from pandanus across northern Australia; identify the materials, their properties, and how they combine with force to create the movement
Test a wheeled toy on different surfaces (timber, carpet, rubber, plastic) — observe and explain differences in movement and speed; connect surface material properties to friction and movement
Explore a marionette or Indonesian wayang kulit shadow puppet — identify how specific materials combine with applied forces to create and control movement
elaborations: investigating First Nations Australians' instructive toys and how such toys are designed and made to produce movement, for example propeller toys made from pandanus across northern Australia
selecting materials to show how material properties are appropriate for particular designed solutions, for example materials that enable sliding, floating or flying
exploring how to manipulate materials using a range of tools, equipment and techniques to create movement, for example when constructing a toy boat that floats or a kite that flies
exploring a system such as a marionette or Indonesian wayang kulit shadow puppet to see that by combining materials with forces movement can be created
testing materials to see how they affect movement and speed, for example the movement of a wheeled toy on different surfaces such as timber, carpet, rubber and plastic

AC9TDE2K03.minimum_width: Name at least one plant and one animal used as a source for food, clothing or shelter; identify at least one product derived from each; identify where one plant or animal is grown in Australia.
AC9TDE2K03.typical_width: Identify plants and animals as sources across food, clothing and shelter categories in different Australian regions; trace products from source to finished item; describe how tools and equipment are used in growing and harvesting.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians grow plants and animals for food — for example the Kombumerri Peoples' aquaculture industry farming mangrove worms, or land transformation through terraces at Wagadagam; identify the plants or animals, the products and the growing methods

Compare growing methods at different scales — home garden tools (spade, rake) versus large-scale equipment (seed spreader, GPS tractor, drones for forestry); explain what each enables and why scale changes the tools needed
Trace a product from source to finished item across the full production chain — for example cotton in NSW from seed to yarn to fabric for clothing
elaborations: exploring how First Nations Australians grow plants and animals for food, for example how land is transformed through the construction of terraces at Wagadagam on Mabuiag Island in the Torres Strait, or how the Kombumerri Peoples of South East Queensland developed an important aquaculture industry farming mangrove worms
identifying which plants and animals can provide food or materials for clothing and shelter, for example looking at a range of items and sorting them according to plant or animal source

exploring where plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter in Australia, for example citrus fruit in South Australia; cotton in New South Wales, which is harvested and made into yarn and fabric for clothing; or timber for building homes from sustainable forests in Tasmania
identifying products that can be designed and produced from plants and animals, for example food products, paper and wood products, fabrics and yarns

considering a range of tools and equipment that can be used to grow plants for a purpose and their suitability, for example naming and describing tools such as a spade or rake used to cultivate or mulch a home vegetable garden, or equipment such as a seed spreader or global positioning system (GPS) tractor to sow wheat, or a tubestock planting tool and drones to manage forestry plantations

AC9TDE2K04.minimum_width: Categorise at least three familiar foods into food groups using the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating; identify at least two preparation methods and explain how one changes the food.
AC9TDE2K04.typical_width: Identify a wide range of foods across the 5 food groups; design a simple menu using multiple food groups; prepare a food product using appropriate tools and techniques; connect preparation choices to healthy eating.
wider: Explore both the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Guide to Healthy Eating — identify foods from both guides across the 5 food groups; compare foods that are familiar to different communities
Explore how people from countries of Asia select and prepare food for healthy eating based on available plants and cultural practices — compare with Australian food selection and preparation contexts
Explore the local supermarket — observe the variety of foods and shelf placement; discuss how display design may influence food selection for healthy eating
elaborations: identifying a wide range of foods, categorising them into food groups according to the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and discussing ways to eat a variety of food groups, including cooking methods, tools and equipment needed to prepare them for healthy eating

exploring how people including peoples from the countries of Asia design and produce food for healthy eating based on the available plants and animals in their region, the influence of cultural practices, and locally available tools and equipment

exploring the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Guide to Healthy Eating and identifying foods in each of the 5 food groups which contribute to health and wellbeing, for example choosing foods from each of the 5 food groups which they are familiar with and designing a menu for a day

exploring the local supermarket to observe the variety of foods and the placement of foods on shelves, in aisles and displays; and considering how their design may influence the purchase of foods for healthy food eating

exploring different ways of preparing the products from the school kitchen garden, farmers' market or supermarket, for example preparing vegetables for a salad, steaming or roasting vegetables and noticing the changes in flavour and texture

AC9TDE2P01.minimum_width: Generate at least one design idea that builds on observations of an existing product; produce a drawing or model with at least one label or description; use at least one digital tool to communicate a design idea.
AC9TDE2P01.typical_width: Compare and contrast existing products to generate new ideas; produce labelled 2D drawings with different views; use digital tools alongside drawing and modelling as part of the design process; communicate opinions about design ideas.
wider: Design a new environment (cubbyhouse or animal shelter) — show different views (top and side) with descriptions of materials and features for each view
Design felt finger puppets after experimenting with toys with movable parts — include labelled drawings showing how movable parts work; record audio or video opinions about design choices
Record taste-test results for a food product using a digital tool — use the results to communicate a revised design decision
elaborations: comparing and contrasting features of existing products to develop new ideas, for example designing and making a puppet with a movable part after experimenting with other toys with several movable parts

communicating design ideas by modelling or producing and labelling 2-dimensional drawings using a range of technologies, for example designing a new environment such as a cubbyhouse or animal shelter and showing different views (top view and side view) with descriptions of materials and features
communicating an opinion about their design ideas, for example expressing own likes and dislikes about a design idea for felt finger puppets including how they have made changes to their design ideas
describing the results from exploring design ideas, for example recording the results from people taste-testing a food product

AC9TDE2P02.minimum_width: Select at least one material with a reason for its suitability; use at least two tools or techniques safely in a construction context.
AC9TDE2P02.typical_width: Select materials appropriate for the design purpose and explain suitability; practise a range of joining techniques and construction skills across multiple making contexts; follow safety expectations consistently; assemble components and check they function.
wider: Explore re-use of available materials (wrapping paper, gift cards, food containers) to make a designed solution — identify how material re-use minimises waste and how properties of re-used materials affect what can be made
Construct a toy boat that floats or a kite that flies — deliberately select materials for their movement-enabling properties; explain each material choice
Make musical shakers — assemble containers, contents and joining materials; check they function as planned; explain why each joining technique was chosen
elaborations: exploring how available materials can be used or re-used in construction play, for example using used wrapping paper and gift cards to design and make decorations or signage for the classroom or a school event to minimise waste
practising a range of technical skills using tools and equipment safely, for example joining techniques when making products, watering and mulching gardens, preparing a recipe using a knife safely
assembling components and checking they function as planned, for example containers, contents and joining materials when making musical shakers

AC9TDE2P03.minimum_width: Describe at least one strength and one area for improvement in a design or solution; identify at least one environmental impact and suggest one way to reduce it.
AC9TDE2P03.typical_width: Evaluate design ideas and solutions using personal preferences across multiple design contexts; reflect on environmental impacts of production; suggest alternative approaches that minimise negative impacts; record evaluations using audio, video or written responses.
wider: Evaluate the environmental impacts of different food packaging options — suggest how packaging could be redesigned to minimise impact; explain the trade-offs between function and sustainability
Share design strengths and weaknesses for a playground — explain how equipment might be unsuitable for some users and suggest specific improvements
Record evaluation of a made solution using audio or video — review the recording and identify at least one thing to change in the next design iteration and why
elaborations: reflecting on and recording a judgement about design ideas, for example describing how design ideas meet the needs of those who will use the solution using audio-recording or video-recording software
sharing design strengths and weaknesses, for example explaining how the equipment in a playground might be unsuitable for some children to use and suggesting areas for design improvement

reflecting on the environmental impacts of the production of a solution and considering alternative approaches that would minimise future negative impacts, for example identifying the negative environmental impacts of different food packaging and how these could be minimised

reflecting on the challenges of designing and producing a solution and recording these reflections, for example when growing a food product, designing a structure to take a load or making a nutritious snack

AC9TDE2P04.minimum_width: Sequence at least four making steps in correct order; carry out an identified role in a cooperative making task.
AC9TDE2P04.typical_width: Use lists or storyboarding to sequence steps for making across different production contexts; identify roles for group members; work cooperatively to produce a shared outcome; adjust steps or roles when problems arise.
wider: Plan and make a number of items for a school event — assign roles (cutting, joining, decorating, checking) and sequence the steps; explain how each role contributes to the shared outcome
Write instructions for making a container or bag including who does each step and in what order — test whether another group can follow the instructions
Create an electronic planting calendar — sequence the planning and planting steps using a digital tool; identify roles for each group member
elaborations: using lists or storyboarding when planning and making, for example when creating an electronic planting calendar
recording the procedure for making a product, for example the ordered steps for making a salad, instructions for making a container or bag
identifying roles for each member of a group when working cooperatively, for example when making a number of items for a school fete
